subtopic_detail: limping toddler with a normal initial tibial radiograph after a low height twisting fall
stem:
You are the registrar in a suburban emergency department. An 18-month-old boy is brought in because he has refused to walk since yesterday afternoon, when he slid off the bottom step of a play fort and his foot caught under him. His mother says he screamed briefly, settled with a cuddle, and has been his usual cheerful self since, but he now crawls everywhere and cries if she stands him up.

He is afebrile and has been eating and drinking normally, with no rash and no recent illness. On examination he lies happily on the trolley and moves both hips and knees through full range without complaint. There is no swelling, warmth or bruising of either leg. He cries reproducibly when you gently rotate the right foot relative to the shin, and settles as soon as you stop. Radiographs of the right tibia and fibula in two planes are reported as showing no fracture.

data_table.Examination: Full painless range at both hips and knees, no joint swelling, warmth or effusion
data_table.Palpation: Distress on gentle torsion of the right tibia, no focal bony tenderness elsewhere
data_table.Investigations: Right tibia and fibula radiographs, two views: no fracture identified

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Request an urgent magnetic resonance scan of the right leg under sedation today
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance would show the fracture line, but it needs sedation at this age and does not change a management plan that is immobilisation either way. It is reserved for the child whose symptoms persist despite immobilisation or whose picture suggests infection. (Source: RCH CPG: Toddler's fracture)

options.text: Arrange an urgent hip ultrasound to look for a joint effusion before discharge
options.rationale: Hip ultrasound is the move when the hip is the painful joint, but this boy moves both hips through full range without complaint and localises to tibial torsion. The near pair is transient synovitis, which restricts internal rotation of the hip and does not reproduce pain on rotating the foot against the shin. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

options.text: Discharge with simple analgesia and advice to mobilise as tolerated at home
options.rationale: Analgesia alone is reasonable when the examination is genuinely normal, but reproducible pain on tibial torsion is a positive finding and unprotected weight bearing on an occult spiral fracture prolongs the limp. A normal first radiograph does not exclude the injury. (Source: RCH CPG: Toddler's fracture)

options.text: Apply an above ankle walking boot and review clinically in seven to ten days
options.rationale: A well child with a torsional mechanism, pain on tibial rotation and no bony tenderness elsewhere has an undisplaced spiral tibial fracture until proven otherwise, and this pattern is invisible on up to half of first films. Immobilisation with clinical review, rather than repeat imaging, is the management whether or not a fracture is later confirmed. (Source: RCH CPG: Toddler's fracture)

options.text: Send blood cultures with inflammatory markers and admit for intravenous antibiotics
options.rationale: A septic workup belongs to the febrile or systemically unwell limping child, and this boy is afebrile, feeding normally and settles the moment the leg is left alone. Treating him as infected commits him to a cannula and admission for a mechanical injury. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

explanation.summary: The toddler's fracture is an undisplaced spiral fracture of the distal tibial shaft caused by a low energy twisting force in a newly ambulant child, typically between nine months and three years. Because the periosteum is thick and the fracture line is often hairline and oblique, initial radiographs miss a large proportion of cases and the diagnosis is made clinically. The differential that matters is infection, so the afebrile, systemically well child with a clear mechanism can be immobilised and reviewed rather than investigated further. Persistent refusal to weight bear at review, fever, or a rising inflammatory response should redirect towards osteomyelitis or septic arthritis. Non-accidental injury deserves consideration when the child is not yet walking independently, because the mechanism requires an ambulant child.
key_points: Low energy torsional mechanism in a newly walking child with refusal to weight bear.
Pain reproduced by rotating the foot against the shin, with no focal bony tenderness.
Up to half of initial radiographs are normal; a normal film does not exclude it.
Immobilise and review clinically; reserve advanced imaging for atypical or persistent cases.
A spiral tibial fracture in a child who cannot yet walk should raise safeguarding concern.
explanation.pearls: Healing periosteal new bone appears on radiographs at about 10 to 14 days, so a repeat film a fortnight later confirms the diagnosis retrospectively if it is ever needed, which is why the plaster goes on before the imaging is conclusive.

subtopic_detail: infant with a persistently watering eye and crusted lashes since the first weeks of life
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 5-month-old boy whose mother says his left eye has watered constantly since he was about two weeks old. Tears spill down the cheek even when he is content, and most mornings the lashes are stuck together with a yellowish crust that wipes away easily with a warm washer. She has been given two courses of antibiotic drops by a colleague, each of which cleared the crusting for a few days before it returned.

He was born at term and is growing along the 50th centile. On examination he fixes and follows your face with each eye covered in turn, and the left conjunctiva is white and quiet with no injection. Pressing over the area between the inner corner of the eye and the nose produces a bead of mucoid material at the lid margin. The corneas are clear and of equal size, and the red reflex is present and symmetrical.

data_table.Examination: Left epiphora with quiet white conjunctiva, no lid or periorbital swelling, no photophobia
data_table.Eye assessment: Red reflex present and symmetrical, corneal diameters equal and corneas clear, fixes and follows with either eye
data_table.Provocation: Mucoid reflux at the punctum on pressure over the lacrimal sac

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management at this visit?

options.text: Commence oral cefalexin and arrange paediatric review within forty eight hours
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics are for acute dacryocystitis, in which the sac becomes red, tense and tender with surrounding cellulitis and the infant is often febrile. Expressible mucoid material from a soft non-tender sac is not infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange urgent ophthalmology review the same day for measurement of intraocular pressure
options.rationale: Same day review is for infantile glaucoma, the important near pair, which also waters but adds photophobia, blepharospasm, corneal clouding and an enlarged corneal diameter. Clear corneas of equal size and a comfortable child make it very unlikely here. (Source: RCH CPG: Nasolacrimal duct obstruction)

options.text: Teach lacrimal sac massage with lid hygiene and review him at twelve months of age
options.rationale: Epiphora from birth with mucoid reflux, a quiet conjunctiva and a normal red reflex is congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction, and around 90 per cent resolve spontaneously during the first year. Massage and lid hygiene with planned review is the correct conservative course. (Source: RCH CPG: Nasolacrimal duct obstruction)

options.text: Refer for probing of the nasolacrimal duct under general anaesthesia within the month
options.rationale: Probing is the correct step, but the timing is wrong: intervention before twelve months treats obstructions that would have resolved on their own and adds an anaesthetic. Probing is reserved for persistence beyond a year or for recurrent dacryocystitis. (Source: RCH CPG: Nasolacrimal duct obstruction)

options.text: Prescribe a further week of chloramphenicol eye drops four times daily and reassess
options.rationale: Topical antibiotic treats bacterial conjunctivitis, which injects the conjunctiva and does not persist for months against a white quiet eye. Repeated courses explain the transient improvement without addressing an anatomical blockage. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction affects up to one in five infants and arises from a persistent membrane at the valve of Hasner at the distal end of the duct. It presents with epiphora and mattering from the first weeks of life, with a white conjunctiva between episodes, and mucoid material that can be expressed from the sac. Two conditions must be excluded before reassurance: infantile glaucoma, which adds photophobia, corneal clouding and enlargement, and acute dacryocystitis, which makes the sac red, tense and tender. Spontaneous resolution occurs in about 90 per cent by twelve months, so probing is deferred until then in the uncomplicated child. Persistent obstruction beyond a year, or recurrent infection of the sac, warrants ophthalmology referral for probing with or without intubation.
key_points: Watering from the first weeks of life with a quiet white conjunctiva suggests duct obstruction.
Expressible mucoid reflux at the punctum supports the diagnosis.
Exclude infantile glaucoma: photophobia, corneal clouding, enlarged corneal diameter.
About 90 per cent resolve by twelve months; massage and hygiene in the interim.
Refer earlier for recurrent dacryocystitis or if signs of glaucoma appear.
explanation.pearls: Crigler massage works by raising hydrostatic pressure in the sac: press firmly over the sac just medial to the inner canthus and stroke downward towards the nose about ten times, twice daily, rather than rubbing the eyelid itself.

subtopic_detail: day one newborn not moving one arm fully after a delivery complicated by shoulder dystocia
stem:
You are the paediatric resident asked to review a term baby boy on the postnatal ward at 18 hours of age. His birth weight was 4320 g and the delivery was complicated by shoulder dystocia relieved with the McRoberts manoeuvre and suprapubic pressure. The midwife has noticed he is not moving his right arm as freely as his left during cares and cries when she dresses him.

On examination he is pink, alert and feeding well at the breast. He grips your finger firmly with both hands and flexes and extends both elbows and wrists spontaneously when he is unwrapped. The right Moro reflex is reduced in amplitude compared with the left. You feel a step and crepitus over the middle of the right collarbone and he grimaces as you do so. The overlying skin is intact with no bruising, and there is no swelling of the arm or forearm.

data_table.Examination: Palpable step and crepitus over the mid right clavicle, intact overlying skin, no arm swelling
data_table.Neurological: Symmetrical palmar grasp, spontaneous elbow and wrist movement bilaterally, asymmetrical Moro
data_table.Feeding: Breastfeeding established, alert and pink between feeds

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Pin the sleeve to the body for three weeks and arrange orthopaedic review in clinic
options.rationale: Strapping the limb is an adult and older child strategy and offers nothing in a neonate whose clavicle remodels completely within weeks. It also restricts the arm movement that keeps the shoulder supple. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal birth injury)

options.text: Reassure the parents, give regular paracetamol and handle the arm gently for two weeks
options.rationale: A mid clavicular fracture after shoulder dystocia with an intact palmar grasp and preserved elbow and wrist movement is a bony injury alone, and these unite rapidly without any intervention. Analgesia and careful handling are all that is required. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal birth injury)

options.text: Request a skeletal survey and notify the child protection team before discharge home
options.rationale: A skeletal survey investigates unexplained fractures, and this one has a documented obstetric mechanism in a macrosomic baby delivered with shoulder dystocia. Escalating to safeguarding for an explained birth injury exposes the family to unwarranted investigation. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Arrange an ultrasound of the shoulder joint to exclude a proximal humeral separation
options.rationale: Ultrasound is useful when the shoulder itself is swollen and the humeral epiphysis may have separated, which produces a pseudoparalysis with swelling and no palpable clavicular step. The palpable crepitus over the collarbone already localises the injury. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Birth injuries)

options.text: Refer urgently to the brachial plexus clinic for nerve conduction studies within the week
options.rationale: Urgent plexus referral belongs to the baby with a true palsy, the key near pair. Obstetric brachial plexus injury abolishes the palmar grasp in lower root lesions or holds the arm adducted and internally rotated in upper root lesions, whereas this baby grips and moves the elbow and wrist. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal birth injury)

explanation.summary: Clavicular fracture is the commonest fracture of birth, occurring in around one to two per cent of vaginal deliveries and far more often when the birth weight exceeds 4000 g or shoulder dystocia occurs. The critical examination task is to separate the bony injury from an accompanying brachial plexus palsy, because the two often coexist and the management differs entirely. Preserved palmar grasp with spontaneous elbow and wrist movement against an asymmetrical Moro points to pain-limited movement rather than denervation. Uncomplicated clavicular fractures need no imaging, no immobilisation and no orthopaedic follow-up, and parents should be warned that a palpable lump of callus will appear within a week or two. Any baby with a genuine plexus lesion needs early referral because the window for surgical assessment is measured in months.
key_points: Macrosomia and shoulder dystocia are the dominant risk factors.
Grip and distal movement distinguish a painful clavicle from a plexus palsy.
No immobilisation, no imaging and no orthopaedic follow-up are needed.
Warn parents about the callus lump appearing at one to two weeks.
Refer early if grip is absent or the arm is held adducted and internally rotated.
explanation.pearls: An asymmetrical Moro reflex on its own does not distinguish fracture from plexus injury, because pain inhibits the reflex; it is the palmar grasp, which is spared in Erb palsy and absent in Klumpke palsy, that tells you which nerve roots are involved.

subtopic_detail: school aged child with nasal symptoms that worsened again after an initial improvement at day seven
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 7-year-old girl brought back by her father. She started with a blocked nose and a cough twelve days ago, was clearly getting better by about day six, and then over the last three days has become worse again with thick discoloured nasal discharge, a daytime cough and a temperature her father measured at home at 38.6 degrees.

She has missed two days of school and complains that her face aches when she leans forward to put on her shoes. She has had no previous sinus problems and takes no regular medications. On examination she is alert and well perfused with moist mucous membranes. There is mucopurulent discharge in both nasal passages and tenderness over both cheeks. The tympanic membranes are pearly and mobile, the pharynx is mildly injected without exudate, and the chest is clear on auscultation. There is no periorbital swelling, no proptosis and eye movements are full and painless.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 98/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees
data_table.Examination: Bilateral mucopurulent nasal discharge with maxillary tenderness, clear chest, pearly mobile tympanic membranes
data_table.Eye assessment: No periorbital swelling or proptosis, full painless eye movements, normal visual acuity

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Provide intranasal saline with analgesia and advise review if not settling in a week
options.rationale: Saline and analgesia alone are correct for the uncomplicated viral illness that is steadily improving, or for symptoms under ten days without double sickening. A documented second deterioration with fever changes the probability enough to treat. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Start intranasal mometasone with an oral decongestant for a seven day course
options.rationale: Intranasal corticosteroid is an adjunct in chronic and allergic rhinosinusitis rather than a treatment for an acute bacterial episode, and oral decongestants are not recommended in this age group. Neither addresses the bacterial infection. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Commence oral amoxicillin and arrange clinical review in forty eight to seventy two hours
options.rationale: Double sickening, a clear improvement then deterioration after day five with fever and purulent discharge, is the pattern that identifies acute bacterial sinusitis rather than a prolonged viral illness. Amoxicillin is the first line agent in Australia and review at 48 to 72 hours catches non-response. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Admit for intravenous ceftriaxone with urgent ophthalmology and otolaryngology review
options.rationale: Intravenous therapy and urgent specialist review are the correct response to orbital or intracranial extension, the complication to fear. Full painless eye movements with no periorbital swelling or proptosis exclude that here. (Source: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

options.text: Refer for a computed tomography scan of the sinuses before deciding on treatment
options.rationale: Sinus imaging is reserved for suspected complications or for surgical planning in recurrent disease, because mucosal thickening is common in well children and does not confirm infection. It would add radiation without changing this plan. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Most paediatric rhinosinusitis is viral and resolves within ten days, so the diagnostic problem is deciding which child has a bacterial infection worth treating. Three patterns justify antibiotics: persistent symptoms beyond ten days without improvement, severe symptoms with fever above 39 degrees and purulent discharge for three or more consecutive days, or double sickening in which a clearly improving illness worsens again. Australian guidance makes amoxicillin the first line, with amoxicillin and clavulanate reserved for treatment failure or recent antibiotic exposure. The complications that drive urgent referral are orbital cellulitis, subperiosteal abscess and intracranial extension, so eye signs and neurological status must be documented at every assessment. Failure to improve within 48 to 72 hours of starting antibiotics should prompt reassessment rather than a simple repeat script.
key_points: Double sickening after day five is a recognised trigger for antibiotic treatment.
Amoxicillin is first line in Australia; escalate only for failure or recent antibiotic use.
Imaging is for suspected complications or surgical planning, not for diagnosis.
Document eye movements, proptosis and visual acuity to exclude orbital spread.
Reassess rather than repeat the script if there is no response by 72 hours.
explanation.pearls: Orbital cellulitis in a child almost always originates from the ethmoid sinuses through the thin lamina papyracea, so painful or restricted eye movement in a child with sinusitis is a surgical emergency rather than a reason to change oral antibiotic.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

subtopic_detail: toddler whose thumb has become fixed in a bent position at the end joint over several months
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 2-year-old girl whose mother has noticed over the past four months that the end of her right thumb stays bent. It was intermittent at first and would click straight when her mother pulled on it, but for the last six weeks it has stayed bent all the time.

There was no injury that anyone recalls. She uses the hand normally for feeding herself and building towers, and does not appear to be in pain. On examination the right thumb is held flexed at the joint nearest the nail and you cannot passively straighten it fully. There is a firm mobile nodule on the palmar surface at the base of the thumb that moves with the tendon. The thumb is warm, pink and not tender, and the skin creases are normal. The left thumb extends fully and there is no nodule. All other digits move normally and she has no joint swelling elsewhere.

data_table.Examination: Fixed flexion at the right interphalangeal joint of the thumb, full passive range at all other digits
data_table.Palpation: Firm mobile nodule over the palmar aspect of the first metacarpophalangeal joint, non-tender
data_table.Systemic: No joint swelling, warmth or effusion elsewhere, normal skin creases

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Inject the flexor sheath with corticosteroid and review the thumb again in four weeks
options.rationale: Sheath injection is an adult treatment for trigger digit and is not used in young children, in whom the pathology is a size mismatch between a thickened tendon and the pulley rather than inflammation. It also requires sedation at this age. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Trigger finger)

options.text: Refer to a paediatric hand surgeon for consideration of release of the tendon sheath
options.rationale: A fixed flexion deformity at the thumb interphalangeal joint with a palpable nodule over the flexor tendon is paediatric trigger thumb, and a contracture that has been fixed for weeks is unlikely to resolve without surgical release of the A1 pulley. Referral avoids a permanent deformity. (Source: RCH CPG: Trigger thumb)

options.text: Reassure the parents that this resolves spontaneously and review her in twelve months
options.rationale: Spontaneous resolution does occur, but rates fall sharply once the deformity is fixed rather than intermittently triggering, and this one has been fixed for six weeks. Waiting a further year risks a stiff joint. (Source: RCH CPG: Trigger thumb)

options.text: Arrange hand therapy for a night extension splint and passive stretching for six months
options.rationale: Splinting and stretching have a role in the intermittently triggering thumb that still extends passively, but they do not reliably correct an established fixed contracture. Six months of therapy delays a definitive procedure without changing the outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: Trigger thumb)

options.text: Request inflammatory markers with an antinuclear antibody and refer to rheumatology
options.rationale: This workup targets juvenile idiopathic arthritis, the near pair when a child holds a digit flexed. Arthritis produces a swollen warm tender joint with morning stiffness rather than a painless nodule that glides with the flexor tendon. (Source: RCH CPG: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis)

explanation.summary: Paediatric trigger thumb is a mechanical mismatch between a nodular thickening of the flexor pollicis longus tendon, called Notta's node, and the A1 pulley at the base of the thumb. Unlike adult trigger finger it is not an inflammatory condition and is only rarely associated with systemic disease, so it presents painlessly and is usually noticed by a parent rather than the child. Most children present with the thumb already fixed in flexion because the earlier intermittent triggering phase passes unnoticed. Spontaneous resolution is reported in a proportion of cases, particularly under one year of age and when the thumb still extends passively, which is why observation is reasonable early and surgery is preferred once the contracture is fixed. Release of the A1 pulley is a short day procedure with a high success rate and low recurrence.
key_points: Painless fixed flexion of the thumb interphalangeal joint in a toddler.
A firm nodule gliding with the flexor tendon at the metacarpophalangeal level.
It is mechanical rather than inflammatory, so corticosteroid injection is not used.
Observation suits the young infant or the passively correctable thumb.
Refer for A1 pulley release once the deformity is fixed.
explanation.pearls: The nodule of paediatric trigger thumb sits at the metacarpophalangeal level rather than at the joint that is bent, so palpating the base of the thumb while passively flexing and extending the tip is what confirms the diagnosis without any imaging.
